n151323450: Imagine building a whole city around a magazine! That's University City. In nineteen-oh-two, a bold publisher named Edward Gardner Lewis bought land just northwest of the fairgrounds for the nineteen-oh-four World's Fair. His headquarters was an ornate eight-sided tower, the Woman's Magazine Building, and in September nineteen-oh-six he incorporated University City and became its very first mayor. Sculptor George Julian Zolnay carved the famous Lion Gates at its entrance. Lewis's empire later collapsed under fraud charges, but his octagon tower lives on as City Hall. Decades later, a new hero arrived. In nineteen seventy-two, Joe Edwards opened Blueberry Hill on Delmar Boulevard and brought the Delmar Loop back to life. In nineteen eighty-eight he started the St. Louis Walk of Fame, bronze stars in the sidewalk for Chuck Berry, Miles Davis and Tina Turner. Chuck Berry, the first person ever inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, played the Duck Room every month until twenty fourteen, and his statue stands across the street. And here's something close to home for us: along the Loop, Gol Bowl serves masala dosa, and House of India adds masala dosa on weekends. Rock and roll, then dosa: perfect pairing!
n151325351: Quick question for the back seat: what was Brentwood called before it was Brentwood? Maddenville! In nineteen nineteen the neighbors here formed a little village so the bigger towns around them couldn't swallow them up, and somewhere along the way the name changed to Brentwood. Ten years later, in April nineteen twenty-nine, it officially became a city. It's tiny, only about eight thousand people, but it has a big story. There was once a close-knit African American neighborhood here called Howard-Evans Place, and families were moved out when the Promenade shopping center was built. People in Brentwood still remember it. The other big story is water: Deer Creek, which runs through town, has flooded the area by Hanley Road more than twenty-five times since nineteen fifty-seven, so the city launched a project called Brentwood Bound to tame the creek and build a greenway trail for walking and biking. Every September, the whole town comes out for the Brentwood Days festival at Rogers Parkway, and its leafy streets earned it a sweet nickname, the City of Warmth. Small town, warm heart, and a creek that's finally learning to behave!
n151364091: Town and Country: the name is the whole plan. Back in eighteen eighty-six this was farm country called Altheim. In nineteen fifty a tiny village of just one hundred sixty-two people decided to stay a mix of town and country, homes tucked between woods and fields, and today it's one of the wealthiest cities in Missouri. But the loudest day in its history was about golf. The famous Bellerive Country Club is here; it hosted the U.S. Open in nineteen sixty-five and the PGA Championship twice. In August twenty eighteen, at the hundredth PGA Championship, Brooks Koepka won with a record score while Tiger Woods charged with a sixty-four on the final day, his best ever last round in a major. The roars rolled across these hills. And here's something close to home for us: just past the city line, across from Queeny Park, is the Hindu Temple of St. Louis, serving thousands of families, with a shrine to Lord Venkateswara. The Telugu Association of St. Louis and the Tamil Sangam, which runs a Tamil school and a Pongal festival, bring together families from all around these suburbs. Mansions, golf and Balaji: quite a neighborhood!
n151601681: Here's a town that was born because of a breakup! In eighteen seventy-six, the city of St. Louis split off from St. Louis County, and the county suddenly had no courthouse and no capital. So two Virginia-born farmers, Ralph Clayton and Martin Hanley, donated their land. On December fourth, eighteen seventy-seven, county voters chose this spot as the new county seat, and a few months later three thousand people gathered to watch the courthouse cornerstone being laid. The town took Ralph Clayton's name, and it became a full city in nineteen thirteen, partly so its neighbor University City couldn't swallow it up. Today Clayton is the county's downtown, with its own little skyline of office towers, courts and lunch spots. And right next door is Washington University, where the national spotlight has landed again and again: its Field House hosted a presidential debate in nineteen ninety-two, and in two thousand eight the famous vice-presidential debate between Joe Biden and Sarah Palin. Even the nineteen-oh-four Olympic Games were held on its athletic grounds. Born from a split, Clayton ended up the place where everyone comes together!
n151890128: Ready for a love story? Creve Coeur is French for broken heart. The legend says a Native American princess fell for a French fur trapper who didn't love her back, and she leapt from a ledge above the lake, and the lake took the shape of a broken heart. Nobody knows if it's true, but the name stuck. For a long time this was just a string of little communities along Olive Street Road. After World War Two, as St. Louis pushed west, Creve Coeur became a city in December nineteen forty-nine. The big news came from business: Monsanto, the giant seed and farm-science company, had its headquarters here until Bayer bought it in twenty eighteen, and Drury Hotels is still based here. Just north is Creve Coeur Lake, the county's oldest park. Back around nineteen hundred, a streetcar line brought city families out to an amusement park called Electric Park, and today rowers glide across the water. And here's something close to home for us: along Olive Boulevard, a restaurant called Tabla serves dosa, idiyappam and thatte idli. A broken heart, mended with a good dosa!
n153348648: Quick quiz: which little town was once the capital of all of Illinois? You're about to drive into it! In eighteen nineteen the old capital, Kaskaskia, kept flooding, so lawmakers built a brand new capital town out here on the prairie and named it Vandalia. For twenty years, until eighteen thirty-nine, the whole state was run from here. The handsome State House you can still visit was built in eighteen thirty-six, and it's the oldest capitol building still standing in Illinois. Now picture a tall young man with a stovepipe hat walking these streets. From eighteen thirty-four, Abraham Lincoln served here as a state lawmaker. This is where his political career began, and where he gave some of his first speeches against slavery. In a park, a big stone even marks a trail Lincoln is said to have walked. Vandalia was also the end of the line for the National Road, America's first federal highway, which started out east and stopped right here in eighteen thirty-nine when the money ran out. On the State House lawn stands the Madonna of the Trail, a pioneer mother with her children, dedicated in nineteen twenty-eight and one of only twelve in the whole country. Wave to her as we roll by, she walked so we could drive!
n153353016: Welcome to Indianapolis, a capital city drawn on paper before anyone lived in it! In eighteen twenty-one, surveyor Alexander Ralston, who had helped plan Washington, D.C., sketched a town exactly one mile square, with a circle in the middle and avenues spreading out like spokes. On January first, eighteen twenty-five, it became Indiana's capital. That circle now holds the tall Soldiers' and Sailors' Monument, finished around nineteen oh one, and it's why people call this the Circle City. Indy has seen big moments. On April fourth, nineteen sixty-eight, Robert F. Kennedy stood on a street corner here and gently told a crowd that Martin Luther King Junior had been killed, asking them for compassion, a speech still remembered today. And in twenty twelve the whole country watched as Indianapolis hosted Super Bowl forty-six, where the Giants beat the Patriots. And here's something close to home for us: the Hindu Temple of Central Indiana, Indiana's oldest Hindu temple, opened in two thousand six, and after a big expansion in twenty fifteen it welcomed seventeen deities, including Lord Subramanya, our Murugan, and Lord Ayyappa. Circle City, full circle!
n153378210: Who's ready for a surprise? Indiana has waterfalls! But first, Cloverdale. The town was laid out in eighteen thirty-nine, and its name is a little picture: clover growing thick in the dales, the open valleys all around. It became an official town in eighteen forty-nine. Just south of here the land turns into wooded hills, and that's where you'll find Cagles Mill Lake, built as Indiana's very first flood control reservoir, with the Lieber State Recreation Area for beaches, swimming and a nature center. Follow Mill Creek a little farther and you reach Cataract Falls, the largest waterfall in Indiana by the amount of water that tumbles over it, with an upper and a lower falls. Right above the falls stands a wooden covered bridge built in eighteen seventy-six, the last covered bridge left in Owen County, now just for people on foot. Back in town, Main Street has artisan shops and summer farmers markets, and the C Bar C Expo Center hosts some of the state's top horse and livestock shows. Clover, horses and a waterfall, Indiana is full of surprises!
n153395278: Mooresville has a hero, a home run, a work of art, and one famous troublemaker! It began with Samuel Moore, a Quaker from North Carolina, who ran a trading post here in eighteen twenty-two, bought land for two dollars an acre, and in eighteen twenty-four laid out a town and named it after himself. Quaker families settled all around, and his wife Eliza founded the town's Methodist church. Since eighteen seventy, folks have gathered every year for the Old Settlers Fair, with a parade right through downtown. The town proudly calls itself the Home of the Indiana State Flag. Baseball Hall of Famer Amos Rusie is tied to Mooresville, and the artist Robert Indiana, famous for his bold LOVE design, went to school at the Mooresville Friends Academy. And the troublemaker? In September nineteen twenty-four a young man named John Dillinger robbed a local grocer here, his first conviction, and he went on to become America's most wanted outlaw. Today you can follow his footsteps on a walking tour from the library. Then cool off at Pioneer Park, with a creek, a pool and a zip line. History with a twist!
n153403193: Take a deep breath, everyone, because this town was named for a smell! Back in the eighteen twenties, Quaker families came all the way from North Carolina, drawn by bubbling mineral springs and wild spicebushes whose leaves smelled sweet and spicy. Hence the name: Spiceland. It became one of the most important Quaker communities in Indiana, and the Friends here built a school, Spiceland Academy, which was incorporated in eighteen seventy and ran until nineteen twenty-one. It was so well known that in eighteen seventy-three, students came from as far as Kansas, Kentucky and even the Sandwich Islands, which we now call Hawaii! Those springs had their own moment too: about a century ago people came here to take the waters, and there was even a sanitarium selling healing spring water until it burned down in nineteen thirteen. The springs still surprise people; in twenty eleven a brand new one popped up and flooded part of a company parking lot! Basketball fans stop by to see the historic old Spiceland gym on the way to New Castle. Fewer than nine hundred people live here today. A small town with a spicy story!
n153410174: Imagine starting a town and, four years later, counting just three houses! That's Brownstown's story. Pioneers had been rolling past on the National Road since a settler named Griffith followed it here in eighteen thirty and built a home a couple of miles west. But the village itself was born in eighteen seventy, when a man named John Brown laid it out, and gave it his name, along the brand new St. Louis, Vandalia and Terre Haute Railroad. The town was only two blocks by four blocks, and by eighteen seventy-four it had just those three houses. Then the trains did their magic and turned little Brownstown into a busy farm community. Later, when cars took over, Route forty through town became a trucker's highway, and the Twin Pumps marker remembers when Dycus Oil and McCoy's Café were among the most popular truck stops on the whole road. McCoy's could seat seventy-eight hungry drivers at once! Today about seven hundred people live here, surrounded by farm fields. From three houses to a truck-stop legend, not bad, Mister Brown!
n153450998: Welcome to the Village of Porches! Look at those old storefronts with porches up on the second floor. This village began in eighteen thirty-three as a settlement called Embarras, right by the river we just crossed. In eighteen thirty-four William C. Greenup laid out the town. He was a big name in early Illinois: clerk of the very first territorial assembly back in eighteen twelve, and later the state's superintendent of the National Road. Travelers stopped at the Barbour Inn, opened in eighteen thirty-one, which stood until nineteen seventy-two. From eighteen forty-three Greenup was the county seat, and a young lawyer named Abraham Lincoln rode the National Road here to attend court, before the seat moved to Toledo in the eighteen fifties. In eighteen seventy the townspeople built their railroad depot, one of the few with living quarters upstairs, and today it's a museum full of model trains and old photos. Nearby you'll find the Abraham Lincoln Well, a Carnegie library, and the longest covered bridge in Illinois. Porches, trains and Lincoln, a perfect place to sit a spell!
n153465063: Ready for a town with a nickname from Oklahoma? This is Saint Elmo, once called the Little Tulsa of Illinois! The story starts in eighteen thirty-four with a tiny stop on the National Road called Howard's Point, a mile west of here. In eighteen sixty-eight four men laid out a new town, and it took its name from a popular book of the day. In nineteen twenty-six Smith Aviation Field opened on the west side, and pilots dropped in, even the famous Charles Lindbergh! In nineteen thirty the town's kids made headlines when the Saint Elmo Juvenile Band finished third in a national contest in Flint, Michigan. Then, in nineteen thirty-seven, came the big news: oil! The Louden field nearby became one of the biggest in Illinois. Workers poured in from Oklahoma, Texas and Kansas, big companies like Shell and Texaco set up shop, and by nineteen forty about three thousand people crowded into town, so many that houses ran short. Gas from the field even heated the town. Keep watching the fields for pump jacks nodding away, still saying hello from the oil boom!
n153467217: Get your cameras ready, because Casey thinks big. Really big! The town was established in eighteen fifty-three and named for Zadok Casey, a lieutenant governor of Illinois who also founded the city of Mount Vernon. In eighteen seventy the railroad arrived, linking Casey to the towns along the National Road. Then oil was found around here, and business boomed so much that the little Casey depot once handled more freight than the station in the big city of Terre Haute! Years later downtown had grown quiet and empty, until a local businessman named Jim Bolin had an idea. His wife and daughter wanted to open a tea shop, so to draw visitors, in twenty eleven he built a wind chime fifty-six feet tall. It became the world's largest, and he kept going: a giant rocking chair, a mailbox you can climb inside, a pitchfork, a golf tee and more, many of them Guinness World Record holders. Soon around five hundred visitors a day were coming to Casey. Big Things, Small Town: proof that one big idea can wake up a whole town!
n153540055: Here's a city that used to be an army base and turned into a forest playground! Back in eighteen forty-nine, two tiny hamlets were laid out along Pendleton Pike. One was called Lanesville, and in eighteen sixty-six it took the name of its post office: Lawrence. For decades it was quiet farm country. Then, in the early nineteen hundreds, the Army bought land here and built Fort Benjamin Harrison, named after the twenty-third president, who came from Indianapolis. Soldiers trained here through two World Wars, and in nineteen seventy the city annexed the fort, even though the Army objected! After the Army left in the nineteen nineties, much of that land became Fort Harrison State Park, about seventeen hundred acres, the biggest forest in central Indiana. Nearly nine hundred thousand people visit every year to hike, bike and fish on Fall Creek, and the Museum of Twentieth Century Warfare tells the fort's story. In April twenty twenty-four the park sat right in the path of a total solar eclipse, with almost four minutes of darkness at midday. And just a few miles south stands the Hindu Temple of Central Indiana, where Diwali is celebrated with fireworks. From marching boots to hiking boots!
n153541146: Welcome to Illinois, everyone, and our first stop over the river has a name that's a little puzzle. Glen Carbon means valley of coal! Long before that, settlers called this land Goshen, after the land of Goshen in the Bible. Then in eighteen ninety-one two companies arrived together, the Madison Coal Company and a brick company, and built a whole company town, with homes and stores for the miners and brick makers. On June sixth, eighteen ninety-two, seventy-six residents signed a petition and Glen Carbon officially became a village. Miners dug coal deep under these hills until the coal company shut down in the nineteen thirties. And here's a fun surprise from history: when people were fixing up an old house here, they found a real pioneer log cabin hidden inside it! It was restored between nineteen eighty-nine and nineteen ninety-two and is now part of the Glen Carbon Heritage Museum. The old railroad lines have turned into bike trails too, like the Nickel Plate Trail and the Heritage Trail named for a former mayor, with signs telling the mining stories. From coal under the ground to bikes on the trails, Glen Carbon keeps its history close!
n153546066: Here's a village whose sports teams are called the Wooden Shoes! Welcome to Teutopolis, the city of the Teutons, the Germans. In eighteen thirty-nine a group of German Catholic families who had first settled in Cincinnati claimed this spot on the National Road and built a little piece of the old country on the prairie. In eighteen fifty-eight Franciscan friars arrived from Germany, the church was renamed Saint Francis of Assisi in eighteen sixty, and in eighteen sixty-two the friars opened Saint Joseph's, a college and seminary that began with fifty-eight students. The seminary later moved to the Chicago area, but a memorial tower still stands where the school used to be. The friars' old living quarters are now the Monastery Museum, thirty-eight small rooms packed with treasures from the friars and pioneers. And those wooden shoes are real history: a man named George Deyman carved wooden shoes for the townspeople for over fifty years, and his tools are now in the Illinois State Museum. The Wooden Shoes are still winning too; in twenty twenty-five the boys golf team won its first ever state title! Clip, clop, wunderbar!
n153564869: Here's a tiny village that couldn't make up its mind about its name! Pocahontas started out as Hickory Grove, then became Amity, and finally in eighteen fifty it took the name Pocahontas, at first spelled with an o in the middle. Around eighteen thirty-one a man named Thomas Stout built a mill on Shoal Creek, which still runs through town beside the railroad, and later coal mining kept families busy for years. In the nineteen sixties the first motel in town, the Powhatan Motel, opened right off the highway, and soon the Powhatan Restaurant opened next door. Both are still serving travelers like us today. Look out for the Old National Hotel too, whose porch columns carry little discs with busts of famous people. And here's the big one: Pocahontas is the hometown of country music star Gretchen Wilson! Its antique shops are famous all over Illinois. Fewer than seven hundred people, but plenty of stories!
n153576099: Our last stop in Illinois is a town where a famous novelist sharpened his pencils! Marshall was founded in eighteen thirty-five by Colonel William Archer and Governor Joseph Duncan, right where the National Road crossed the road from Chicago to Vincennes, and it was named for Chief Justice John Marshall. By eighteen thirty-eight it had grown big enough to win the county seat. Archer was quite a character: a captain in the Black Hawk War and, in eighteen fifty-six, one of the men who backed Abraham Lincoln for vice president at the first Republican convention. In eighteen forty-one the Archer House opened as a stagecoach stop, and it's called the oldest hotel in Illinois still in business! Now the big story: from about nineteen fifty, the Handy Writers' Colony at the edge of town trained more than a hundred writers, and its star, James Jones, author of From Here to Eternity, built a house here and wrote his next novel, Some Came Running. Just south of town, Lincoln Trail State Park remembers the route Lincoln's family took from Indiana into Illinois. Goodbye Illinois, hello Indiana!
n153582081: Here's a town that has always been about crossing paths. Effingham calls itself the Crossroads of America, and it earned that name long before the interstates. Back in eighteen thirty-one the old National Road was pushed through here, carrying pioneers west. Then in eighteen fifty-four the Illinois Central Railroad arrived and crossed that very road, and a sleepy spot once called Broughton suddenly took off. In eighteen fifty-nine the people voted to make it the county seat, and they literally moved the buildings over from the old seat, Ewington, which faded away. Who was the town named for? That's a little mystery! Some say a British lord, Lord Effingham, others say a surveyor named Effingham, and nobody has written proof either way. Today two big highways, I-fifty-seven and I-seventy, meet here, and right at that junction rises the Cross at the Crossroads, one hundred ninety-eight feet of white steel, finished in two thousand one, with stone tablets of the Ten Commandments at its feet. Effingham also raised some stars: radio singer Jack Berch, NBA center Uwe Blab, and Yankees pitcher Chad Green. Roads, rails and big dreams, all crossing in one friendly town!
n153597367: Engines on, everyone, we're entering a town named after a racetrack! In nineteen oh nine Carl Fisher and three partners opened the Indianapolis Motor Speedway. Its first surface of crushed stone and tar was too dangerous, so they paved it with about three point two million bricks, and that's why people call it the Brickyard. In nineteen twelve Lem Trotter bought the land around the track and laid out a brand new town called Speedway, planned as a horseless city for the people who built cars. Today a one-yard strip of those old bricks still marks the finish line. Here's a tasty tradition: in nineteen thirty-six winner Louis Meyer asked for a glass of buttermilk, a photographer snapped it, and now every Indy five hundred winner drinks milk! Since nineteen ninety-six, winners have also knelt down to kiss the bricks. And here's something close to home for us: in two thousand five, Narain Karthikeyan from Coimbatore in Tamil Nadu finished fourth in the Formula One race on this very track, making him the first Indian driver ever to score Formula One points. Vroom vroom, and a toast of milk!
n153597929: Here's a little place that was planned to be a busy town, and then decided to stay cozy instead. Back in eighteen thirty-one a pioneer named George Woodbury built a log cabin right here beside the brand new National Road, and the spot took his name. Two years later Levi Beals built a cabin too, and he became the postmaster, so the mail carrier and tired travelers would stop at his place. In eighteen thirty-five William Greenup, the same man who founded the town of Greenup just up the road, laid out Woodbury with fifty-two lots, twenty-six on each side of the National Road. For years D. T. Wisner kept a small store and post office here. But the big town never quite came. By eighteen eighty-four the old county history said Woodbury was hardly a village anymore, living on mostly in people's memories and in the name of Woodbury Township, created in eighteen sixty. Today it's a quiet community on Route forty with Woodbury Lake nearby. Small place, long memory!
n153665901: Want to hear about the day a president landed in the mud? First, the town. Quaker families came here from North Carolina in the eighteen twenties, people who believed in living plain and simple, so when Levi Jessup and Elias Hadley laid out the town in eighteen thirty-nine, it became Plainfield. The National Road ran right through, and it's still Main Street today. In eighteen fifty-eight the Western Yearly Meeting of Friends was set up here, and Quakers still gather at its meetinghouse. Now the mud: in June eighteen forty-two, former President Martin Van Buren was riding a stagecoach through here, and the driver tipped him right out into the muck, they say to protest his veto of money to improve the road! The elm tree that did it became famous as the Van Buren Elm. Today Plainfield is a busy hub near the Indianapolis airport, home to about half of central Indiana's warehouse jobs. And here's something close to home for us: Indian families have made this area home, and just next door in Avon stands a Hindu temple of the BAPS Swaminarayan community, built in two thousand four. Plain name, colorful story!
n153672061: What do horse races, oil tanks and a giant anvil have in common? Martinsville! Joseph Martin moved to Clark County in eighteen thirty-two and founded this town, and two years later the National Road came through, carrying pioneers right down Main Street. The oldest house still standing here, the Chancellor House, sits by the National Road, near the old York Trail and the railroad line, three ways to travel in one spot! Back in the eighteen hundreds Martinsville was known for horse racing. Then came the big news of the early nineteen hundreds: oil! The Ohio Oil Company became the town's biggest employer, and between nineteen oh six and nineteen oh eight it built two hundred twenty-five oil tanks on twelve hundred acres just west of town. Today you can visit the Lincoln School Museum, a one-room schoolhouse showing what school was like over a hundred years ago. And keep your eyes open on Mill Street for a giant anvil and a big horseshoe, cousins of the big things in Casey just down the road. Small town, strong as iron!
n153704521: Altamont means high ground, and in flat Illinois even a little hill gets noticed! The name came from J. W. Conlogue, a superintendent on the Vandalia Railroad, who looked at the rise of land, the mound, just northwest of town and named the place after it. Trains made this town. Three railroads came through, the Vandalia and Ohio, the Chicago and Eastern Illinois, and the Mississippi line, and Altamont became a busy hub. Daniel Boyer built the first hotel in eighteen seventy-one, and a bank followed in eighteen seventy-six. The grandest house in town belonged to Dr. Charles Wright, one of the only doctors in this part of the county, who also ran the town's bank. His tall Italianate mansion, finished in eighteen eighty-nine, is now a museum you can tour. Just east of town, the Ballard Nature Center spreads over two hundred seventeen acres of trails, the dream of Ernie Ballard, who wanted a place where everyone could enjoy and learn about nature. And if you're hungry, Schultz's Dairy Bar is famous for tenderloin sandwiches so huge they hang off the plate! High ground, big sandwiches, happy travelers!
n153708627: Who here knows the rag doll Raggedy Ann? Her name was born right here, in a way. Greenfield was chosen as the seat of brand new Hancock County on April eleventh, eighteen twenty-eight, set along the National Road, and the county was named for John Hancock, the man with the giant signature on the Declaration of Independence. The town was probably named for an early settler, John Green. On October seventh, eighteen forty-nine, a boy named James Whitcomb Riley was born here, and he grew up to be the Hoosier Poet, loved all over America. Two of his poems, Little Orphant Annie, which came out in eighteen eighty-five, and The Raggedy Man, in eighteen eighty-eight, gave cartoonist Johnny Gruelle, a friend of Riley's family, the idea to blend them into one name for his rag doll: Raggedy Ann! You can tour the Riley Boyhood Home on Main Street. And every October, starting the first Thursday, the whole downtown throws the Riley Festival, with a parade and a theme picked from one of his poems. In twenty twenty-four they celebrated his hundred and seventy-fifth birthday. A town that rhymes with fun!
n153724548: Here's a riddle: what shape can you recognize in the dark, just by touch? A Coca-Cola bottle, and it was invented right here in Terre Haute! But first, the story. Terre Haute means high land in French, for the bluff above the Wabash River. In eighteen eleven soldiers built Fort Harrison here, and in September eighteen twelve, during the War of eighteen twelve, its small garrison held out for days against a siege. The town was laid out in eighteen sixteen, and the river, the National Road and later the Wabash and Erie Canal made it a crossroads. Now that bottle: in nineteen fifteen Coca-Cola asked for a bottle you could know by feel, and the Root Glass Company here won with its famous curvy design. Eugene V. Debs was born here in eighteen fifty-five and ran for president five times, once from prison; his home is now a museum. And in nineteen seventy-nine, a quiet star named Larry Bird led the Indiana State Sycamores, undefeated at thirty-three and oh, into the national championship game against Magic Johnson, still one of the most-watched college games ever. Curvy bottles and big dreams!
n153791229: Want to hear about the silliest machines ever made in Illinois? First, a little history. Greenville is the county seat of Bond County, and it's old: its first church went up in eighteen eighteen and its post office opened in eighteen nineteen, the year after Illinois became a state. In eighteen fifty-five two founders, Stephen Morse and Almira Blanchard, opened Almira College, a college just for women, and in eighteen ninety-two the Free Methodists bought it and named it Greenville College. Since twenty seventeen it's been Greenville University. Even Abraham Lincoln came to visit, invited by his friend Jediah Alexander, who owned the local newspaper. Now for those silly machines! Also in eighteen ninety-two, the DeMoulin Brothers started a company making prank machines for lodge initiations, chairs and gadgets built to surprise and tease new members. Today the same company makes marching band uniforms, and the DeMoulin Museum shows off a whole corral of those old gag devices, drawing visitors from all over the country. Greenville also has the American Farm Heritage Museum and the Richard Bock sculpture museum. From prank chairs to parade uniforms, Greenville never takes itself too seriously!
n153803569: Guess what this little village used to be called? Bucktown! And Houston! And, my favorite, Shakerag! The old county history tells how one of the first settlers, John Bilyew, kept a little post office sitting among lots of mulberry trees, and that's how the prettier name, Mulberry Grove, finally stuck. A post office was running by eighteen thirty-four, Francis Gill laid out the streets in eighteen forty-one, and in eighteen fifty-seven it became an official village. It grew up right on the old National Road, the great highway that carried wagons west, and a historical marker here called the Shake Rag Stop remembers those days. Back then the road turned to deep mud, so the shops on Main Street had sidewalks to keep shoppers' feet out of the muck. On the north side of town Owl Creek wanders past and joins Hurricane Creek just to the east. About five hundred people live here today, under a name much sweeter than Shakerag!
n153808849: Welcome to Indiana, the Hoosier State! Yes, we've crossed the state line, and our first town is West Terre Haute, sitting on the west bank of the Wabash River. Samuel McQuilkin laid it out in eighteen thirty-six, and it was first called McQuilkinsville, then Macksville. In eighteen ninety-four the townspeople voted for the name it has today. And part of town has the funniest name on our whole trip: Toad Hop, named, the story goes, for all the toads hopping and frogs jumping! But the river has a serious side. In March nineteen thirteen a terrible tornado struck the area, and just days later a record flood buried many houses here up to the second story in gravel. Now, a story of courage: in eighteen forty, a French nun named Mother Theodore Guérin arrived in the woods near Terre Haute after three months of travel and founded the Sisters of Providence and a school for girls that became Saint Mary-of-the-Woods College. In two thousand six she was made a saint, Indiana's very first! Toads, floods and a saint, what a welcome to Indiana!
n153841803: Turn up the music, folks, we're rolling into the Cradle of Recorded Jazz! The story starts quietly, though. In eighteen oh six a group of Quakers, mostly from North Carolina, crossed into the new Indiana Territory and founded Richmond, and it grew into the center of a big Quaker settlement. One founding family, the Starrs, later ran the Starr Piano Company down in the Whitewater Gorge. In nineteen seventeen the company started its own record label, Gennett Records, and that little studio by the river made history. In nineteen twenty-three, King Oliver's Creole Jazz Band, with a young Louis Armstrong on cornet, made their very first records right here, some of the earliest jazz ever recorded. Bix Beiderbecke, Jelly Roll Morton and Hoagy Carmichael came too. Today you can stroll the Gennett Walk of Fame along the gorge trail, where the greats are honored right in the pavement. And if you need some quiet after all that jazz, Hayes Arboretum has four hundred sixty-six free acres, with old forest trees that are up to four hundred fifty years old. From Quaker hymns to hot jazz, Richmond's got rhythm!
n5336773606: Here's a name with a secret older than St. Louis itself. Des Peres means of the fathers in French. Around December seventeen hundred, a band of Kaskaskia people and French settlers, with Jesuit priests, the fathers, set up a little mission by a river near the Mississippi. It's believed to be one of the very first European settlements in all of Missouri. The mission lasted only about three years, but the river kept the name, River des Peres, and the name kept traveling. When this area became a town in nineteen thirty-four, nobody even suggested another name; everyone already called it Des Peres. Fast forward to nineteen sixty-nine: West County Center opened here, a mall that became the big weekend outing for West County families. It closed in two thousand one and was rebuilt as a brand-new mall the very next year. And here's something close to home for us: just a short drive west is the Hindu Temple of St. Louis, where Diwali ends with fireworks lighting up the temple grounds, and on Manchester Road you can find Indian kitchens like Flavors. Priests, prayers and fireworks: Des Peres has always been about the fathers, and the families!
n569768151: Here comes Chesterfield, and it's a comeback story. Not long ago this was quiet farmland in west St. Louis County, and it only became a city in nineteen eighty-eight. Five years later came the night nobody here forgets. July thirtieth, nineteen ninety-three, the Great Flood: the Missouri River smashed through the Monarch Levee, and the whole valley, once nicknamed Gumbo Flats, filled with more than eight feet of muddy water. People came back, built higher levees, and the valley grew bigger than ever, with one of the largest strip malls in America. Now the fun part: Faust Park, with the Butterfly House, where thousands of butterflies float around you, and the old St. Louis Carousel. Right there stands Thornhill, built in eighteen nineteen, the oldest governor's home still standing in Missouri. It belonged to Frederick Bates, the state's second governor, whose brother Edward became Abraham Lincoln's Attorney General. And here's something close to home for us: Indian families have been moving to Chesterfield for jobs, and just down the road is the Hindu Temple of St. Louis, which has a shrine to Lord Venkateswara, our Balaji. So yes, you can get darshan near a butterfly house!
n6215791685: Happy Thanksgiving, everyone, because we're rolling past one of the most Thanksgiving towns in America! Webster Groves grew up along the Pacific Railroad, when train tracks let city families live out among the trees. It was first called just Webster, until folks found out Missouri already had a town by that name, so the groves got added. Then in eighteen ninety-six, five little neighborhoods, Webster, Old Orchard, Webster Park, Tuxedo Park and Selma, joined together into one city. Today it's home to the main campus of Webster University. But here's the big news, and it's happening today: every Thanksgiving since nineteen-oh-seven, Webster Groves and neighboring Kirkwood high schools play the Turkey Day Game, one of the oldest Thanksgiving football rivalries in the whole country. Last year Kirkwood won forty-five to fourteen, so the Webster Statesmen are hungry for more than turkey this morning! And here's something close to home for us: a little south of here, in Mehlville, a place called Madhuram's Kitchen cooks gongura pulao straight from Andhra. Football, turkey and gongura: now that's a Telugu Thanksgiving!
n6281417974: Okay, everyone, look out the window, because Weldon Spring has a secret. Picture the seventeen-nineties: a frontiersman named John Weldon builds a log home beside a bubbling spring here, on land Spain still owned. A quiet farm country grows up around it. Then, in World War Two, the Army arrives, moves out three whole little towns, Howell, Hamburg and Toonerville, and builds what was called the largest explosives factory in America, cranking out TNT. In nineteen fifty-five a uranium plant follows. When the country finally cleaned it all up, a story that made national news, they sealed the waste inside a giant stone-covered hill, seventy-five feet tall, finished in two thousand one. And here's the twist: today families climb the stairs to the top just for the view, and the old factory land has turned into the Busch and Weldon Spring conservation areas, with deer, lakes and the Katy Trail along the Missouri River. And something close to home: here in St. Charles County, one Indian family has opened their backyard every Diwali for more than ten years, lighting lamps with their neighbors. From TNT to diyas, not bad for one little spring!
n7504571159: Everybody look up, because here comes the big one: St. Louis! The story starts in the winter of seventeen sixty-four, when a French fur trader named Pierre Laclede and a fourteen-year-old boy, Auguste Chouteau, picked a bluff above the Mississippi for a trading post and named it after King Louis the Ninth of France. Here's a funny twist: that same December the news finally arrived that France had already secretly handed this land to Spain! Laclede died in seventeen seventy-eight, and young Chouteau grew up to become the town's leading citizen. Long before them, the Mississippian people built so many earthen mounds here that St. Louis got the nickname Mound City. It became the jumping-off point for the West, hosted the World's Fair in nineteen-oh-four, and gave the world music legends like Chuck Berry, Miles Davis and Tina Turner. Watch for the shining Gateway Arch on the riverfront. And here's something close to home for us: Indian Americans are now the region's largest group of immigrants. The Telugu Association of St. Louis throws a big Ugadi celebration every spring, the Tamil Sangam celebrates Pongal, and the Hindu Temple out west serves over fourteen thousand Hindus. Namaste, St. Louis!
w167111554: Look down, everyone, this quiet stream has a heroic past! This is the Little Wabash River. It starts west of Mattoon, gets dammed up to make Lake Mattoon, then winds about two hundred forty miles south until it meets the big Wabash River down where Illinois touches Indiana and Kentucky. Now picture February seventeen seventy-nine, in the middle of the American Revolution. George Rogers Clark and his small band of frontiersmen are marching through freezing winter to surprise the British fort at Vincennes. Far downstream from here they reach the Little Wabash and find it flooded into a sheet of icy water about five miles wide! They build a big canoe, ferry their supplies across, and wade on, sometimes up to their shoulders, and a few days later they capture the fort. This river still floods: in May two thousand two, the gauge near Effingham hit its highest flow ever recorded, more than twenty-four feet deep. Yet in many dry summers it barely flows at all. Little river, big moods, and one very brave crossing!
w169382766: Here comes a river with an embarrassing name! It's spelled Embarras, but folks here say AM-braw. French explorers called it embarras, their word for an obstacle, because logjams kept blocking their canoes. This river starts south of Urbana in Champaign County and wanders about one hundred ninety-five miles south, past Charleston, where a dam makes Lake Charleston, and past Fox Ridge State Park, just a few miles from the Lincoln Log Cabin, the farm where Abraham Lincoln's father and stepmother lived. Far downstream, in the freezing February of seventeen seventy-nine, George Rogers Clark's soldiers had to splash across the flooded Embarras on their famous march to Vincennes. And right here near Greenup, the old National Road crossed on a wooden bridge that washed away in eighteen sixty-five, so people rode a ferry for about ten years. Today a two-hundred-foot covered bridge stands on that same spot, rebuilt in the style of the old one, the longest covered bridge in Illinois. So many stories for one embarrassed little river!
w200813905: Let me tell you about a girl who started with nothing and built an empire. Sarah Breedlove was born in eighteen sixty-seven on a cotton plantation in Louisiana, to parents who had been enslaved, and she was an orphan by the age of seven. She grew up to create her own hair-care products, took the name Madam C. J. Walker, and in nineteen ten moved her business to Indianapolis. She became one of the first Black women in America to become a millionaire, and gave thousands of women jobs selling her products. She died in nineteen nineteen, and her daughter A'Lelia finished this building in her memory. The Walker Theatre opened on December twenty-sixth, nineteen twenty-seven, a triangle-shaped Art Deco beauty with fifteen hundred seats, where Indiana Avenue's jazz musicians played. By the nineteen seventies it was closed and falling apart, but people saved it, and in nineteen ninety-one it became a National Historic Landmark. After a fifteen million dollar renovation finished in twenty twenty-one, the street outside was renamed Madam Walker Memorial Way. Big dreams can start very small!
w613113573: Here's the river that decided where Indiana's capital would be! This is the White River. Long before the city, the Lenape people lived along its banks north of here, and the Miami called it Wapahani, meaning white sands. In eighteen twenty, state commissioners picked the spot where the White River meets Fall Creek for a brand new capital, hoping steamboats would sail right up to it. One steamboat, the Robert Hanna, did make it, but it ran aground on the way back, and no steamboat ever returned. So the river became a place to enjoy instead of a highway. Today downtown, White River State Park lines its banks with the Indianapolis Zoo, the Eiteljorg Museum of Native American and Western art, the Indiana State Museum, and a canal walk where you can ride a gondola. The river has had hard times too: in December nineteen ninety-nine, a factory spill upstream killed millions of fish. People fought back, restocking and restoring, and by twenty eleven surveys counted fifty-seven kinds of fish again. A river that bounced back, just like a good road trip after a wrong turn!
